carousels.name: 'I've got this' - overconfidence is a trigger

slides.title: The first few days felt easy. [[That's the trap.]]
slides.sub: Why "I've got this" is one of the most dangerous thoughts in recovery.

slides.title: The [[easy]] start
slides.body: Motivation is high. Urges are quiet. It feels like you've already won. Many people say this is exactly when they drop their guard.

slides.title: Then the [[wave]] hits
slides.body: Around day 4 or 5, many describe a sudden surge of urges. It feels like it came out of nowhere. It didn't — the habit was waiting.

slides.title: Confidence ≠ [[protection]]
slides.body: Feeling strong doesn't mean the blocker can come off or the phone can come back to bed. Keep the guardrails up on the good days too.

slides.title: Stay humble, [[stay clean]]
items: Keep every guardrail — even when it feels unnecessary.
Expect the day-5 wave and plan for it.
Check in daily, not just on hard days.
Treat good streaks as practice, not proof.
slides.note: When did your first big wave hit? Comment the day 👇

slides.title:
Strong days build habits.
[[Systems protect them.]]
slides.lead: A blocker that stays on, daily check-ins and a panic button for the wave you didn't see coming.

carousels.name: Flatline or something more? When to get help

slides.kicker: Read this if you feel numb
slides.title: Is it the flatline — or [[something more?]]
slides.sub: How to tell, and when it's time to talk to someone.

slides.title: What people [[call]] the flatline
slides.body: Low libido, low energy, feeling flat — often a few weeks in. It's a community term, not a medical diagnosis, and many describe it as temporary.

slides.title: When it might be [[more]]
slides.body: Feeling hopeless, losing interest in everything, or struggling to get through the day for weeks. That can look like the flatline — but it can also be depression.

slides.title: Asking for help is [[strength]]
slides.body: A doctor or therapist can help you figure out what's going on. You don't have to tough out low mood alone. Recovery is easier with support.

slides.title: Talk to a professional [[if]]
items: Low mood lasts more than two weeks.
You've lost interest in things you used to enjoy.
Sleep or appetite has changed a lot.
You have thoughts of hurting yourself — reach out today.
slides.note: Save this and send it to someone who might need it.

slides.title:
Recovery isn't
[[a solo mission.]]
slides.lead: An AI coach to talk things through, an anonymous community and guided lessons. RezenIt is self-help, not a substitute for professional care.

carousels.name: Talk to yourself like your best friend

slides.title: You'd never talk to a friend [[the way you talk to yourself.]]
slides.sub: Why self-hate keeps you stuck — and what to say instead.

slides.title: "I'm [[disgusting.]]"
slides.body: That voice feels like accountability. It isn't. Shame tends to push people back to the habit for relief — it feeds the loop.

slides.title: What you'd tell a [[friend]]
slides.body: "You slipped. That doesn't erase your progress. What happened, and what do you need?" Kind and honest, at the same time.

slides.title: Compassion is [[not]] an excuse
slides.body: Being kind to yourself doesn't mean pretending it's fine. It means staying in the fight instead of quitting on yourself.

slides.title: Rewrite the [[voice]]
items: "I'm weak" → "I'm learning."
"I'll never change" → "I'm changing slowly."
"I ruined it" → "I can restart right now."
"I'm disgusting" → "I'm a person with a habit."
slides.note: Which line do you need to hear today? Comment it 👇

slides.title:
Shame-free progress.
[[That's the whole idea.]]
slides.lead: Journal honestly, track progress without judgment and lean on a community that gets it.

carousels.name: You don't need fewer urges. You need more people.

slides.title: You don't need fewer urges. [[You need more people.]]
slides.sub: Why isolation and this habit go hand in hand.

slides.title: The habit [[loves]] isolation
slides.body: Alone in your room, nobody to talk to, nothing on. Many people say their urges were loudest when they felt most disconnected.

slides.title: Connection [[fills]] the gap
slides.body: Real conversations, shared plans, people who expect you somewhere. The need underneath the urge often is the need to feel connected.

slides.title: Start [[smaller]] than you think
slides.body: You don't need a big friend group tomorrow. One call. One plan. One message that says "want to grab food?"

slides.title: This week, [[try]]
items: Text one old friend you've lost touch with.
Join one group: gym class, sport, club.
Work from a café or library once.
Say yes to one plan you'd normally skip.
slides.note: Who's one person you'll message today? (No names needed) 👇

slides.title:
Never feel alone
[[in this again.]]
slides.lead: An anonymous community, 1-on-1 accountability with real people and daily check-ins.

carousels.name: Working from home alone? The 3 PM trap

slides.title: Working from home alone is a [[relapse setup.]]
slides.sub: Nobody around, a laptop all day, and the 3 PM slump.

slides.title: No one [[around]]
slides.body: No coworkers, no commute, no one walking past your screen. The privacy that makes remote work comfortable also removes the brakes.

slides.title: The [[3 PM]] slump
slides.body: Tired, bored, procrastinating on a hard task. A "quick break" on the same device you work on is one click away from trouble.

slides.title: Your [[bed]] is your office
slides.body: Working from bed blurs every line. Your brain stops knowing what that space is for — and the old habit fills the blank.

slides.title: Remote-work [[rules]]
items: Work at a desk, never in bed.
Blocker on during work hours too.
Take breaks away from screens — walk, stretch, water.
Leave the house once a day, no matter what.
slides.note: WFH people: when's your hardest hour? Comment it 👇

slides.title:
Make your home
[[a safe space.]]
slides.lead: Turn your devices into a safe, distraction-free space and track every clean workday.
